PHSCS 587

Ballistic injection and backscattering

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how reflected carriers reduce net velocity relative to an injection-speed scale

A short channel is not automatically described by the long-channel mobility law. Injection from contacts and scattering that returns carriers toward the source can determine the net current. Ballistic means negligible scattering through the relevant transport region, not infinite speed.

In a simple two-population picture, set the incident population to one and reflected population to r, with speed magnitudes vT in opposite directions. Net flux is proportional to vT(1 − r), total population to 1 + r, and vnet = vT(1 − r)/(1 + r).

At r = 0 the net velocity equals the injection-speed scale. The formula assumes a particular distribution and equal speed magnitudes; real contacts and energy-dependent transmission require a fuller transport model. In the ballistic limit, increasing a bulk mobility parameter is not the same as improving injection.

Example

For r = 0.25, the normalized net velocity is 0.75/1.25 = 0.60. Reducing r to 0.10 raises it to about 0.818; this ratio alone does not specify charge density or total current.

Sources and scope
  • PHSCS 587 reading: 6.3–6.3.3.1, preceding ballistic/backscattering discussion

Practice

1. Why does the denominator contain 1 + r while the numerator contains 1 − r?

Velocity is net directional flux divided by total population.

Returning carriers subtract from the forward flux but still add to the number of carriers present. Dividing those quantities gives (1 − r)/(1 + r).
